query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, thermally stable and corrosion‐resistant surface coating (for example, an alumina film deposited via atomic layer deposition) on the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA will suppress surface degradation mechanisms, thereby improving its long-term creep behavior and corrosion resistance without degrading its inherent strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure produced by conventional casting.
generation.intervention: Deposit a conformal, ~50 nm thick alumina (Al2O3) coating on the alloy surfaces using atomic layer deposition (ALD).
generation.conditions: Expose coated and uncoated specimens to cyclic thermal fluctuations (room temperature up to 700°C), long-term room-temperature loading (to assess creep under sustained stress), and corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions) that mimic conditions for aircraft/space fasteners.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent alumina layer that acts as a diffusion barrier and passivation film on the alloy's surface.
generation.mechanism: The alumina coating limits surface oxidation, reduces the ingress of corrosive species, and inhibits surface diffusion and microcrack initiation during thermal cycling and sustained loading. This barrier effect helps preserve the bulk microstructure while reducing creep deformation and corrosion attack at the surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit enhanced corrosion resistance and improved long-term creep behavior under cyclic and sustained loading conditions while retaining a comparable strength–ductility balance to the uncoated baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-cast (or thermomechanically processed) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA without any surface coating.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits are expected within the service temperature range up to ~700°C and in moderately aggressive corrosive environments; extreme mechanical impact or environments beyond these conditions may not yield the same level of improvement.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term adhesion and stability of the thin coating under repeated thermal cycling and sustained mechanical stresses remain to be fully established, and the optimal coating thickness and processing parameters may require further refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy specimens intended for aerospace fastener applications. One set will be coated with a ~50 nm alumina film via ALD while the other set will remain uncoated. Subject both sets to (1) accelerated cyclic thermal aging (cycling between room temperature and 700°C for 100 cycles), (2) long-term creep testing under constant stress at room temperature for 1000 hours, and (3) corrosion testing in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions under standardized conditions.
measurements: Measurement of tensile/yield strengths and ductility before and after testing
Quantification of creep deformation (strain vs. time) under constant load
Electrochemical corrosion rate testing (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization)
Microstructural and interfacial analysis (using SEM, EDS, and possibly TEM) to assess coating integrity and substrate degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance (lower creep strain) and reduced corrosion rates compared to the uncoated specimens, or if the coating fails by delaminating or degrading under thermal cycling, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD (calculation of phase diagrams) method can also provide an insightful guidance to design EHEAs, on the premise that reliable thermodynamics database for HEAs are to be established and completed. In summary, here we proposed a novel strategy to design high-entropy alloys (HEAs), i.e., the concept of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), to solve the challenging issues for this new type of advanced metallic materials, including the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility, and the inferior castability and compositional segregation. Based on the new strategy, we successfully designed a highly uniform AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, with an unprecedented combination of castability, high fracture strength and high ductility. The bulk EHEA ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared by the conventional casting method using the commercially pure raw materials. The EHEA exhibited a fine lamellar microstructure consisting of coupled grown fcc/B2 phases. Our design strategy is of great significance in both scientific and technical aspects, and can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs.

The high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a new alloy with more than four main elements. In recent years, HEAs have attracted attention due to their outstanding performance, including superior mechanical properties, abrasion resistance, and corrosion resistance [,]. Single-phase body-centered-cubic (BCC) and face-centered-cubic (FCC) HEAs have been the subject of much research over the past decade. Several studies have reported that BCC HEAs possess high strength, while FCC HEAs are highly ductile. According to comprehensive research, it is difficult to achieve both high strength and ductility in single-phase HEAs [,,]. To further improve the properties of HEA, Lu et al. [,] proposed the concept of eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) that combined the strength of BCC HEAs and ductility of FCC HEAs. EHEAs have broad application prospects due to their excellent mechanical properties over a wide temperature range [,,]. However, EHEA research mainly focuses on mechanical properties, while there are few studies on the corrosion behavior of EHEAs.
